claims.text: The exceptional combination of strength and ductility in HEAs under high-strain-rate loading is primarily caused by local atomic disorder impeding dislocation mobility.
Inhibition of dislocation mobility by local atomic disorder enhances strain-rate sensitivity.
Inhibition of dislocation mobility delays dynamic recovery.
Inhibition of dislocation mobility promotes sustained work hardening relative to less compositionally complex alloys.
Atomic-scale chemical disorder and its associated lattice distortions act as pinning points for dislocations.
Local atomic disorder creates a rugged energy landscape in HEAs.
The rugged energy landscape impedes dislocation glide.
The rugged energy landscape impedes dislocation cross-slip.
Under dynamic loading, the HEA will show a larger increase in flow stress with strain rate than the conventional-alloy baseline.
The HEA will exhibit more pronounced strain-rate dependence of yield stress than the conventional-alloy baseline.
The HEA will exhibit delayed dynamic recovery relative to the conventional-alloy baseline.
The HEA will exhibit enhanced work hardening under dynamic conditions relative to the conventional-alloy baseline.
The proposed mechanism produces a superior combination of strength and ductility compared with conventional alloys.
The conventional-alloy baseline can have a similar average elemental composition to the HEA while having lower configurational entropy and less local atomic disorder.
The proposed disorder-controlled mechanism should apply from roughly room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures and from quasi-static rates to approximately 10^3 s^-1.
At cryogenic temperatures or extremely high strain rates, alternative mechanisms may dominate the dynamic response.
